title: AYT
subtitle: Lessons from a failed high-end personal shopping venture: a business model that works in one industry may not transfer to another.
html:
Taking e-commerce experience into another industry

After operating the computer studio, I tried a personal shopping business focused on fashion and premium goods. Although both were e-commerce businesses, product selection, customer trust, pricing, and logistics required a different understanding. The venture failed.

A broad product range without a clear position

I began with fashion and premium products because demand appeared substantial. That also placed me in a crowded market. Without a sufficiently clear niche or selection theme, I struggled to give customers a compelling reason to choose my service.

Pricing and customer acquisition reinforced each other

I tried setting service fees in line with the market, but similar pricing was not enough to attract orders. The business had little visibility, few reviews, and limited word of mouth, making it difficult to build a stable customer base.

Low order volume also affected logistics. I could not reach the shipment thresholds needed for more favorable rates, so international shipping increased the overall price and made the service less competitive.

The judgment I took from the failure

A business model that works in one industry may not transfer to another. Before entering a new market, I need to re-examine demand, differentiation, trust, and logistics costs rather than assume that the approach from an earlier success will work again.
